"Profusely" means in a very large amount — so much that it is hard to ignore, hard to control, or even hard to stop. It is a stronger, more vivid way of saying "a lot" or "very much," but with a specific flavor: the amount is so great that it stands out, feels overwhelming, or almost overflows.

When you say something happens "profusely," you're saying it doesn't just happen — it happens in full force, in striking abundance, well beyond what is ordinary.
The feeling behind the word

Picture a tap that won't stop running, or a garden so full of flowers that you can barely see the leaves beneath them. That sense of overflowing — of too-much-ness — is exactly what "profusely" captures.

It's not just "he sweated a bit." It's "he sweated profusely" — rivers of sweat, soaking through his clothes, impossible to miss.

It's not just "she thanked me." It's "she thanked me profusely" — thank you after thank you, warm, generous, and perhaps even a little overwhelming.
How it is used — the three main situations

"Profusely" is an adverb, meaning it describes how something happens. It usually comes right after the verb it modifies.

1. Physical or bodily actions — things the body does in large, often uncontrollable amounts:

  • He was sweating profusely after the run. (Rivers of sweat, noticeably so.)
  • The wound was bleeding profusely. (A large, alarming amount of blood.)
  • She cried profusely at the funeral. (Tears flowing without stopping.)

2. Expressions of emotion or social gestures — especially gratitude, apology, and praise:

  • She thanked him profusely for his help. (Again and again, with deep sincerity.)
  • He apologized profusely for arriving late. (Many apologies, deeply felt.)
  • They praised her profusely after the presentation. (Enthusiastically and repeatedly.)
3. Natural growth or decoration:

• The roses bloomed profusely this spring. (An abundance of blooms, more than usual.)
  • The walls were decorated profusely with paintings and tapestries.
  • He wrote profusely throughout his life, leaving behind hundreds of letters and journals.
What makes "profusely" different from simply saying "a lot"?

You could say "he sweated a lot" or "she thanked me a lot" — and the meaning would be similar. But "profusely" does something extra:

  • It is more formal and literary.
  • It paints a vivid, striking picture — the excess feels dramatic, almost cinematic, not just mild.
  • It often hints that the amount is hard to control or hard to contain.

"He sweated a lot" gives you plain information. "He sweated profusely" makes you almost feel the discomfort.
Degree — where it sits on a scale

Think of it like this:

a little → somewhat → a lot → greatly → profusely

"Profusely" sits near the very top. It is not quite "infinitely," but it is clearly well beyond "a lot." The amount is so large that it is striking, noticeable, and possibly difficult to stop.
The tone — formal or casual?

"Profusely" is a formal to semi-formal word. You will find it often in novels, news writing, and serious prose. In casual everyday speech, people tend to say "a lot" or "so much" instead. But using "profusely" in conversation is not odd — it simply sounds more expressive and deliberate, like you're choosing your words carefully.
What "profusely" does NOT mean

• It has nothing to do with speed — not quickly, not slowly.
  • It has nothing to do with quality — it only speaks to amount or degree.
  • It does not mean "secretly" or "quietly." Things done "profusely" are almost always visible, audible, or otherwise noticeable.
  • It does not mean "carefully" or "skillfully."
Close synonyms — and how they differ

Several words are similar to "profusely," but each has its own shade:

  • Abundantly — similar, but a bit more neutral and positive. Implies plenty of something good. ("The land was abundantly fertile.")
  • Copiously — very close to "profusely," perhaps even slightly more clinical. Works especially well for liquids, notes, or data. ("She took notes copiously.")
  • Lavishly — adds a sense of luxury or extravagance, spending freely. ("The room was lavishly furnished.")
  • Excessively — clearly negative in tone; too much, beyond what is right or reasonable. ("He talked excessively.")

"Profusely" sits in the middle of these: it captures the large, striking amount vividly, without automatically judging it as bad or good.
Is "profusely" positive or negative?

Neither, by default. The word itself is emotionally neutral — the situation gives it its color:

  • "She thanked me profusely." → Warm and positive.
  • "He was bleeding profusely." → Alarming and negative.
  • "The garden bloomed profusely." → Beautiful and positive.
  • "He apologized profusely." → Could be genuine remorse, or nervous over-apologizing — depends on context.
A few more examples to fully anchor it

• The athlete perspired profusely under the afternoon sun.
  • Despite his best efforts, he blushed profusely when she called his name.
  • Despite the heavy fog, the meadow was blooming profusely with wildflowers.
  • After the surgery, the patient was bleeding profusely through her bandages.
  • The crowd cheered profusely when the team scored in the final second.
  • He illustrated his point profusely with examples, diagrams, and stories.
  • She was sweating profusely, her hands trembling before the speech.
One-sentence summary to remember it by
"Profusely" means in a strikingly large, hard-to-ignore, often hard-to-stop amount — beyond ordinary, and usually impossible to miss.
